Find the R equivalent of a Stata command

Source: R/findit.R
findit.Rd

findit() looks up a Stata command and returns the R code that does the same job, whether a tidystata function or one from another package. It covers everyday data work (browsing, tabulating, generating, merging, reshaping) and points to the packages tidystata leaves to others, such as fixest for reghdfe, modelsummary for esttab, binsreg for binscatter and srvyr for svy.

It also works the other way round: give it an R function, such as findit(left_join), and it describes the function and lists the Stata commands it replaces. Beginners need not know which is which; a word that is both, such as log or round, shows both meanings.

Type a single word bare, as in findit(reg), add names and hints with commas, as in findit(tab, sex, region) or findit(tab, gen), or quote full Stata syntax, as in findit("merge 1:1 id, keep(match)"). Call findit() with no argument for the whole list.

Usage

findit(command = NULL, ...)

Arguments

command

A Stata command or an R function name, either one bare word (findit(tab), findit(left_join)) or a quoted string (findit("bysort g: egen m = mean(x)")). R functions may also be written as lm() or dplyr::left_join. Use !! to look up a string stored in a variable: findit(!!cmd). NULL (default) returns every entry.

...

Unnamed variable names and command hints, captured without evaluation. Names customize examples in Stata operand order, including new output variables: findit(xtile, quartile, income). A bare hint such as gen selects the generate() option. Hints match exactly or by an unambiguous prefix of at least three letters. Quote a name to use it literally when it conflicts with a hint, as in findit(tab, "gen"). Use !! for a name stored in a string. Calls, numbers, missing arguments and named arguments are not accepted here.

Value

A tibble with one row per Stata idiom and the columns match ("stata" when the word is a Stata command, "r" when it is an R function used in the entry, "keyword" for a text match, "nearest" for the closest entries to a plain question, "all" for the whole list), stata (the Stata code), r (equivalent R code), package (where the R function lives) and task (what it does). It prints each entry as a short block: what it does, then the Stata code and the R code on lines labelled Stata: and R:, so the code is never cut off. The package column identifies the primary package; namespace-qualified helper calls may require additional packages. When one entry answers the query, only that entry is printed. Routine commands have a canonical default, such as tabulate x for findit(tab). Up to five examples are printed when different meanings or structural choices remain unresolved, such as the direction of reshape. Hidden examples are always counted, with a line to run for the rest, such as findit(tab) |> print(n = Inf). The returned tibble always has every match, so it can be stored, filtered or opened with View(). Headings use a single #, without an introductory summary. R-function notes already demonstrated or resolved by comma-separated inputs are omitted. Supplied names customize compatible examples; examples requiring different variables retain all their original placeholders. No matches are removed. A note identifies retained placeholders when those examples are displayed, or explains when no example fits. If nothing matches, a message suggests similar names and an empty tibble is returned invisibly.

Details

Matching follows fixed rules, without any guessing:

  • The first word is looked up both as a Stata command and as an R function. Stata's minimum abbreviations work: reg, regr and regress all find regress; su and sum find summarize; ta and tab find tabulate. R functions must be named in full (lm finds lm() but not glm()); upper and lower case are ignored only when no exact name matches.

  • Entries found as a Stata command come first. Entries found only through the R function follow. A description is added only when the function does not appear in a displayed example. Hundreds of R functions are described, including many that no entry uses yet, such as n_distinct() or fct_relevel(); for those, findit() prints the description and the related Stata command.

  • A leading by ...: or bysort ...: prefix is set aside, so findit("bys g: sum x") looks up summarize and lists the grouped entries first.

  • The remaining words put the best-matching entries first. For example, findit("merge keep(match)") lists inner_join() before the other merge entries, and findit("mutate egen") lists the egen entries among the many that use mutate(). Among equally good entries, the one with the fewest further words comes first. All matching entries are still returned.

  • Comma-separated names and hints select among these examples and fill their recorded variable roles. Variable lists can accept several names, while fixed roles must all be supplied. Dataset names, function names and unrelated constants are unchanged. Strings that represent column names or formulas are customized too. R names are quoted as needed; non-Stata names are shown with backticks in the reference Stata line. This is a lookup over existing examples, not a parser or executor for arbitrary Stata programs.

  • If a hint prefix has several interpretations, competing examples are shown. If no example satisfies every hint, the closest alternatives are shown with an explanation. For plain questions a uniquely highest-ranked meaning is shown alone; tied meanings retain up to five representative examples.

  • If neither matches, the text is searched for in the Stata code, the R code and the task, so findit(winsor) and findit(dummy) also work.

  • Otherwise the text is read as a plain question, in English or Chinese, and the closest entries are listed under their own heading: findit("how do I remove duplicate rows"). The closest entries are the ones sharing the most informative words with the question, after common words are dropped and a short built-in list of synonyms is applied ("average" also means "mean"). A question of three or more words that happens to start with a command, such as findit("count how many people in each category"), lists the closest entries first. No language model is involved, so the same question always gives the same answer.

R reads a call before findit() runs, so anything that is not a single R name must be quoted: several words ("merge 1:1 id"), reserved words ("if"), and names starting with an underscore ("_n").

When R runs in Chinese (the LANGUAGE environment variable or, if it is unset, the locale), the task and function descriptions are shown in Chinese, and Chinese keywords are searched in any language. Sys.setenv(LANGUAGE = "en") switches back to English, as it does for R's own messages.

The list is curated rather than exhaustive. Longer explanations, in English and Chinese, are in the "Coming from Stata" articles on the package website.

Nonempty notes and qualifications print with their examples, including legacy workflows. Explicit expansion also prints reference links. Reference packages are needed only when running their examples; lookup stays offline and does not load or install them. A qualification identifies supplied option combinations absent from the curated examples. Known unsupported queries are explained explicitly. The reference articles distinguish canonical commands, Stata functions and operators, Stata examples and alternative R approaches. Example metadata uses stable IDs, so several R implementations may share the same Stata syntax without losing their variable-role annotations.

tidystata and statar can be attached together; only tab() and xtile() share names. Attach tidystata last, or write tidystata::tab().

Examples

findit(reg)
#> # Linear regression [stats]
#> Stata: regress y x1 x2
#> R:     fit <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = data)
#> # Note: summary(fit) shows the coefficient table; broom::tidy(fit) returns it as a data frame.
#> 
#> # 17 more examples. To see them all: findit(reg) |> print(n = Inf)
findit(su)
#> # Summary statistics for all variables [tidystata]
#> Stata: summarize
#> R:     summ(data)
#> # Note: summary(data) is the base R version, with a less tidy layout. summ() also reports missing counts and has its own default statistic layout; select .stat explicitly when matching Stata output.
#> 
#> # 6 more examples. To see them all: findit(su) |> print(n = Inf)
findit(tab, sex, region)
#> # Two-way cross-tabulation [tidystata]
#> Stata: tabulate sex region
#> R:     tab2(data, sex, region)
#> # Note: fre2(data, x1, x2) adds row and column totals. tidystata retains missing categories by default; Stata tabulate excludes them unless missing is specified. Use .missing = FALSE to match Stata.
#> 
#> # 20 more examples. To see them all: findit(tab, sex, region) |> print(n = Inf)
findit(tab, gen)
#> # Dummy variables for every category [tidystata]
#> Stata: tabulate x, generate(x_)
#> R:     as_dummy(data, x)
#> # Note: as_dummy(data, x, .names = "index") numbers the columns x_1, x_2, ... as Stata does. Also: fastDummies::dummy_cols(data, "x"). as_dummy() defaults to value-based column names; .names = "index" gives numbered Stata-style suffixes. Check the missing-category indicator policy too.
#> 
#> # 20 more examples. To see them all: findit(tab, gen) |> print(n = Inf)
findit(xtile, quartile, income)
#> # Quantile groups [tidystata]
#> Stata: xtile quartile = income, nquantiles(4)
#> R:     mutate(data, quartile = xtile(income, 4))
#> # Note: xtile() follows Stata's rule, so equal values stay in the same group.
#> 
#> # 2 more examples. To see them all: findit(xtile, quartile, income) |> print(n = Inf)
findit("merge 1:1 id, keep(match)")
#> # Keep matched rows only [dplyr]
#> Stata: merge 1:1 id using data2, keep(match)
#> R:     inner_join(data1, data2, by = "id")
#> # Note: dplyr retains overlapping non-key columns with suffixes instead of Stata master values, creates no _merge, and does not enforce a declared 1:1 key constraint.
#> 
#> # merge() [base]: Merge two data frames (base R)
#>   Related Stata: merge
#> 
#> # 17 more examples. To see them all: findit("merge 1:1 id, keep(match)") |> print(n = Inf)
findit("bys g: egen m = mean(x)")
#> # Group statistic as a new variable [dplyr]
#> Stata: bysort group: egen x_avg = mean(x)
#> R:     mutate(data, x_avg = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), .by = group)
#> # Note: For an all-missing group mean(..., na.rm = TRUE) gives NaN; Stata egen mean() gives numeric missing. Normalize NaN if that distinction matters.
#> 
#> # 59 more examples. To see them all: findit("bys g: egen m = mean(x)") |> print(n = Inf)
findit(winsor)
#> # Winsorise at the 1st and 99th percentiles [datawizard]
#> Stata: winsor2 x, cuts(1 99)
#> R:     mutate(data, x_w = datawizard::winsorize(x, threshold = 0.01))
#> # Note: datawizard uses R quantile cutpoints while winsor2 uses Stata percentile rules; small samples and ties can therefore yield different caps.
#> 
#> # Cap both tails at explicitly selected empirical quartiles [base]
#> Stata: gstats winsor x, cuts(25 75) generate(z)
#> R:     bounds <- stats::quantile(data$x,c(.25,.75),na.rm=TRUE,type=2); data$z <- pmax(bounds[1],pmin(bounds[2],data$x))
#> # Note: Unweighted workflow with an explicit R type-2 empirical percentile rule; no cross-software numerical certification is claimed.
#> 
#> # Set values outside empirical quartiles to missing [base]
#> Stata: gstats winsor x, cuts(25 75) trim generate(z)
#> R:     bounds <- stats::quantile(data$x,c(.25,.75),na.rm=TRUE,type=2); data$z <- data$x; data$z[!is.na(data$x) & (data$x<bounds[1] | data$x>bounds[2])] <- NA_real_
#> # Note: Trimming sets tails to missing while retaining rows; percentile rule is explicit R type 2 and no weighted parity is asserted.
#> 
#> # Cap tails separately inside each group [dplyr]
#> Stata: gstats winsor x, by(g) cuts(25 75) replace
#> R:     data <- dplyr::mutate(data,x={b <- stats::quantile(x,c(.25,.75),na.rm=TRUE,type=2); pmax(b[1],pmin(b[2],x))},.by=g)
#> # Note: Groups use independent unweighted R type-2 cutoffs; all-missing groups require an explicit policy.

# Plain questions
findit("how do I remove duplicate rows")
#> # Closest entries for "how do I remove duplicate rows"
#> 
#> # Drop rows that duplicate an earlier row [tidystata]
#> Stata: duplicates drop
#> R:     duplicates_drop(data)
#> 
#> # 9 more examples. To see them all: findit("how do I remove duplicate rows") |> print(n = Inf)

# R functions work too, and words with both meanings show both
findit(left_join)
#> # Keep all rows of the master data [dplyr]
#> Stata: merge 1:1 id using data2, keep(master match)
#> R:     left_join(data1, data2, by = "id")
#> # Note: dplyr retains overlapping non-key columns with suffixes instead of Stata master values, creates no _merge, and does not enforce a declared 1:1 key constraint.
#> 
#> # 3 more examples. To see them all: findit(left_join) |> print(n = Inf)
findit(log)
#> # Record console output in a file [base]
#> Stata: log using results.log
#> R:     sink("results.log")
#> # Note: Most R users write an R Markdown or Quarto report instead of a log.
#> 
#> # Natural logarithm [base]
#> Stata: generate y = ln(x)
#> R:     mutate(data, y = log(x))
#> # Note: log10() matches Stata's log10(). R's log(0) is -Inf rather than missing. R log(0) gives -Inf and a negative input gives NaN with a warning; Stata ln() gives numeric missing for these invalid inputs.
#> 
#> # 9 more examples. To see them all: findit(log) |> print(n = Inf)

# The whole list
findit()
#> # Find the R equivalent of a Stata command [tidystata]
#> Stata: findit command
#> R:     findit(command)
#> # Note: Bare words and comma-separated names work: findit(tab, sex, region). Add hints such as findit(tab, gen), or quote full Stata syntax. One clear example is shown by default; print(n = Inf) reveals every match. findit() with no argument returns the whole list.
#> 
#> # Open the help page of a function [utils]
#> Stata: help command
#> R:     help(function_name)
#> # Note: ?function does the same. In RStudio you can also search the Help pane.
#> 
#> # Search all installed help pages [utils]
#> Stata: search keyword
#> R:     help.search("keyword")
#> # Note: ??keyword is a shortcut. To find the R version of a Stata command, use findit().
#> 
#> # Remove a dataset from memory [base]
#> Stata: clear
#> R:     rm(data)
#> # Note: Rarely needed: R holds many tables at once, each under its own name.
#> 
#> # Show the working directory [base]
#> Stata: pwd
#> R:     getwd()
#> 
#> # 1777 more examples. To see them all: findit() |> print(n = Inf)
